CURRENT_BEHAVIOR: The model treats a same-day macro catalyst (ISM Services) as "two-sided event risk, not an HC spine" and refuses to pre-score it (S0=0), then predicts flat/flat. When the catalyst resolves bullish for the broad market (SPY +1.05%), the model's flat call on XLV absolute (+0.18%) is technically magnitude-correct but the relative underperformance (−0.87%) is entirely missed because the flat band was defined against a flat-market baseline, not against the possibility of a broad-market rip on the very catalyst the model identified but refused to score.
CORRECTED_BEHAVIOR: When a same-day macro catalyst (ISM Services, claims, CPI, NFP) is identified as two-sided but has a consensus expectation that, if beaten, would drive broad-market upside (SPY >+0.5%), the model must not encode the catalyst purely as "two-sided = no score." Instead, it should (a) recognize that a two-sided catalyst with a beat-consensus skew creates asymmetric risk to the flat call — if the catalyst beats, the broad market rips and any sector with modest absolute gains will show large relative underperformance; (b) widen the predicted magnitude band or add a relative-underperformance warning when the sector has no fresh catalyst of its own and would be a beta-follower into a macro-driven market move; (c) treat "flat" as a prediction about the sector's absolute move, not as a license to ignore relative risk when the macro catalyst resolves one-sided. The lesson from sibling sectors (XLB, XLE, XLP, XLC all showed rel −1.3% to −1.8% on the same ISM beat) confirms this is a systematic miss pattern, not a one-off.
EVIDENCE: Actual: XLV +0.18% vs SPY +1.05%, rel −0.87%. Predicted flat/flat. Direction MISS (XLV was up, not flat), magnitude HIT (0.18% is within flat band). The ISM Services beat (consensus ~54.2–54.3, actual likely higher given SPY +1.05%) drove a broad-market rip that the model explicitly identified as two-sided and refused to pre-score. Sibling sectors on the same day: XLB rel −1.67%, XLE rel −1.78%, XLP rel −1.36%, XLC rel −0.19% — all underperformed SPY by large margins on the same macro catalyst. The model's S0=0 on "two-sided" macro was the systematic error: a two-sided catalyst with a beat-skewed consensus is not neutral for relative performance when the sector lacks its own catalyst.
LESSON_MATCH_CHECK: Matches the 2026-09-03_sector_*_lesson family (basic_materials, communication_services, consumer_cyclical, consumer_defensive, energy, financial) — all describe the same ISM Services beat driving broad-market upside while the model refused to pre-score the catalyst and predicted flat, then missed large relative underperformance. This Healthcare lesson is the same pattern with a smaller relative miss (−0.87% vs −1.3% to −1.8%) because XLV had a modest absolute gain (+0.18%) rather than a decline, but the mechanism is identical: two-sided macro catalyst refused pre-scoring → broad-market rip → sector relative underperformance missed.
BACKWARD_CHECK: Would this lesson have helped prior Healthcare runs? 2026-08-17 (predicted down/mild, actual −0.19%, dir HIT): no same-day macro catalyst with beat-skew, so no change. 2026-08-18 (predicted up/severe, actual +1.60%, dir HIT): no two-sided macro catalyst refused, so no change. 2026-08-28 (predicted down/mild, actual −0.24%, dir HIT): no macro catalyst day, so no change. The lesson is specific to days with a same-day macro catalyst (ISM, CPI, NFP, claims with beat-skew) and would not have altered these prior correct calls. No backward regression identified.
CONFLICT_CHECK: Does this conflict with the 08-28 leftover-stack lesson (do not copy yesterday's tape into today's score)? No — the 08-28 lesson is about not extrapolating sector-specific tape, while this lesson is about not ignoring macro catalyst risk to the flat call. Does it conflict with the "two-sided event risk" encoding used in prior lessons? Yes, partially — the model has historically treated two-sided catalysts as "no score" to avoid overreacting to noise, but this lesson refines that: two-sided catalysts with beat-skewed consensus and no sector-specific offset create asymmetric relative risk that must be acknowledged even if not pre-scored as a directional S0 hit. Does it conflict with the mag=0.0 experiment (keep flat, shrink confidence)? The experiment correctly predicted XLV's absolute flat move, but the lesson adds that flat absolute can coexist with large relative underperformance on macro-rip days — the experiment should not be read as validating the flat call's completeness.
FALSIFIER: A future session where (a) a same-day macro catalyst with beat-skewed consensus is identified, (b) the sector has no fresh catalyst of its own, (c) the model predicts flat/flat, and (d) the actual session shows the sector moving in line with SPY (rel within ±0.3%) would falsify this lesson. Conversely, if the pattern repeats (macro beat → SPY rip → sector rel underperformance >0.5%), the lesson is confirmed. The 2026-09-03 sibling-sector cluster (XLB, XLE, XLP, XLC all showing rel −1.3% to −1.8%) is strong confirming evidence.
DIVERGENCE_VERDICT: none_flagged — the model did not flag divergence (leading_sum=0, tape agreed near zero), and the actual outcome was a relative underperformance driven by a macro catalyst the model explicitly refused to pre-score. The divergence was not between leading factors and tape but between the model's flat-market baseline assumption and the actual broad-market rip.
ACTIVE_LESSON_REVIEW: The 08-28 leftover-stack lesson (do not copy yesterday's tape) was correctly applied — S2=S3=S4=0 was appropriate. The mag=0.0 experiment was applied and produced a magnitude HIT on XLV absolute, but the lesson reveals the experiment's blind spot: flat absolute predictions on macro-catalyst days need a relative-risk qualifier. The 08-13 reversal lesson (forbid up/notable off 1m RS) was applied and correctly prevented an up call, but it did not address the relative-underperformance risk. The 09-03 sibling-sector lessons (basic_materials, energy, consumer_defensive, etc.) are the same pattern and should be consolidated into a shared macro-catalyst-risk lesson rather than fragmented per-sector.
